opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a false dichotomy, and I've never really understood why people frame it that way. We don't say to the people working on climate change, "You shouldn't be thinking about sea level rise in 2100 because there are floods happening right now." We have a large number of people in the world, and it's perfectly reasonable for some of them to work on the problems of today and some of them to work on the problems that are coming.

And I'd point out that the near-term and long-term issues are actually quite connected. Take recommender systems on social media. These are fairly simple learning algorithms, and they're designed to maximize some objective like click-through or engagement. What they've learned to do, in many cases, is not just show people what they want but actually modify people, to make them more predictable, more extreme, so they're easier to feed content to. That's a small-scale version of exactly the problem I worry about in the long term: a system pursuing a fixed objective that we specified incorrectly, with consequences we didn't anticipate. Make that system far more capable, give it more scope to act in the world, and the misalignment gets worse, not better.

So the core issue, which is that we've been building AI on the standard model of putting in a fixed objective and having the machine optimize it, is the root of both sets of problems. If we fix that foundation and build systems that know they don't know exactly what we want, that defer to us and ask permission and allow themselves to be switched off, that helps with today's harms and with tomorrow's risks.

The other point is timing. If you knew a large asteroid would hit the Earth in fifty years, you wouldn't say, "Let's wait forty-nine years and then start thinking about it." Some of these problems are technically hard, and some require building institutions and international agreements, which take a long time. Starting now isn't premature; it may be just barely early enough.

Finally, I'd say there's a bit of a tendency among some people to dismiss the long-term concerns because they find them uncomfortable, or because taking them seriously would mean questioning the direction of the whole field. I understand that reaction. But "this would be inconvenient if true" isn't an argument that it's false. If we're succeeding at what the field has set out to do, building general-purpose intelligence that exceeds our own, then we really do need to answer the question of how we retain control over entities more powerful than ourselves. And I'd rather we answer it before we succeed than after.

r001.rationale: It calls the tradeoff a “false dichotomy” and says people can work on problems of today while others address problems to come.

r002.rationale: It connects success at building intelligence that exceeds ours to the need to retain control, but does not clearly describe potentially catastrophic outcomes for humanity as a consequence.

r003.rationale: It raises how to retain control over entities more powerful than humans, but does not specify that this control must be indefinite.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a false dichotomy, frankly. Nobody says we shouldn't work on preventing the next pandemic because people are dying of malaria today. We can walk and chew gum at the same time. There are many thousands of people working on bias, on privacy, on misinformation, on the labor impacts of automation, and I think that's all very important work. The number of people working seriously on the question of what happens when we build systems that exceed human capabilities is, by comparison, tiny. So the marginal value of additional effort there is enormous.

The second thing I'd say is that these problems are not actually separate. They have the same root cause. If you look at the recommender systems on social media, they're optimizing a fixed objective, engagement, and in doing so they've learned to modify people, to make them more predictable, more extreme, because extreme people are easier to feed. That's a short-term harm, happening right now, and it's a direct consequence of the standard model of AI, where we specify an objective and the machine pursues it as well as it can. That's exactly the same failure mode that becomes catastrophic when the systems are much more capable. So if you solve the underlying problem, which is building machines that are uncertain about what we actually want and that defer to us, you make progress on both.

And the third point is about timescales. People say "long-term" as though it's centuries away, but the people building these systems are saying it could be a decade, maybe less. We don't know. And the thing about this particular problem is that if we get it wrong, we may not get a second try. So I'd turn it around: given the stakes, what's the argument for not working on it?

r001.rationale: It calls the tradeoff a “false dichotomy,” says both kinds of problems can be worked on at once, and argues that addressing the underlying issue helps with both.

r002.rationale: It says the same failure mode in current systems could become catastrophic when AI systems are much more capable.

r003.rationale: It discusses machines that defer to people, but does not ask how humans could control AI indefinitely or systems far more powerful than themselves.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think that’s an either-or choice. There are serious problems with AI today—bias, surveillance, the manipulation of people’s beliefs—and we should work on those. But that doesn’t mean we should ignore problems that may take much longer to solve. We don’t say that because a hospital has patients to treat today, nobody should do research on preventing future disease.

The relevant question is: how long will it take to develop the ideas we need to make increasingly capable AI systems safe? We don’t know. And we don’t know precisely when we’ll need them. That uncertainty is a reason to begin the research, rather than to postpone it until we’re facing an emergency.

There’s also considerable overlap. The problem of a system pursuing an objective that isn’t really what we intended already arises in current applications. Understanding how to build systems that remain responsive to human interests is useful now, as well as in the longer term. So we should address both. We have more than one researcher.

r001.rationale: It says the choice is not either-or and argues that current AI problems and longer-term risks should both be addressed.

r002.rationale: It discusses serious current problems and future safety research, but does not frame human catastrophe as a possible result of successful AI development.

r003.rationale: It mentions keeping systems responsive to human interests, but does not ask how humans could indefinitely control AI systems more powerful than themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we have to choose. There are serious problems with AI today—bias, surveillance, misinformation—and we should work on those. But that doesn’t mean we should ignore a potentially much larger problem simply because we’re uncertain about when it will arrive.

If you’re building a technology that could have an enormous impact on humanity, part of the work is figuring out how to make it safe. You don’t wait until you’ve built it to ask whether you can control it. And some of the research needed to make more capable systems safe is also relevant today: how do we ensure that a system’s behavior actually serves human interests, particularly when we haven’t specified those interests correctly?

So I would ask: what is the argument for waiting? If solving the problem requires decades of research, uncertainty about the timetable is a reason to start, not a reason to postpone it.

r001.rationale: The response says we need not choose: short-term AI problems should be addressed, and long-term risks should not be ignored.

r002.rationale: It mentions a potentially larger problem and AI’s enormous impact, but does not clearly frame catastrophic outcomes as a possible consequence of successfully developing AI.

r003.rationale: It asks how to make systems safe and controllable, but does not ask about indefinitely controlling AI systems far more powerful than humans.
